observations.quote: How the True Physick, which is covered bark and rind, is to be got out, and rightly prepared by Fire
observations.note: The chapter heading names its subject: how the True Physick is got out of what covers it and prepared by Fire.

observations.quote: which is covered bark and rind
observations.note: The heading says the True Physick is covered, with bark and rind as the covering; it has to be got out.

observations.quote: ALL things in respect of the first matter were created perfect, but the Chymist perfecteth the last matter by Fire
observations.note: First matter was created perfect; the last matter the Chymist perfects by Fire.

observations.quote: The Physitian perfecteth the Creature of God by Fire.
observations.note: The margin note gives to the Physitian the perfecting by Fire that the paragraph gives to the Chymist.

observations.quote: nothing in this lower world (which is subject to generation and corruption) is so noble but hath Poyson in it selfe
observations.note: Everything in the lower world, however noble, has Poyson in itself, and the Physick lies very near it.

observations.quote: where there is hurt there is also help, where there is venome there is vertue
observations.note: In God's chief works hurt and help, venom and virtue stand in the same place.

observations.quote: which the sublunary Elements bring forth, should alwayes be joyned together in all things, to put us dayly in mind of the Fear of God
observations.note: Good and evil are joined in all things by Nature's ordering, to remind us daily of the Fear of God.

observations.name: Eccl.
observations.note: Croll's margin note names Eccl. 39.26 beside the words on Good and Evill joined in all things; the text gives no verb of saying, so the words stay ruled as Croll's.

observations.quote: As soon as the Omnipotent gave Power to Man, presently he raised up an enemy, least the Power growing lazy should loose its Nature
observations.name: Firmianus
observations.note: Words the text gives to Firmianus: an enemy was raised up together with man's power, so that the power should not grow lazy.

observations.quote: as the Poet said, nothing is in every respect happy
observations.name: the Poet
observations.note: A saying given to an unnamed Poet; the lines given do not show which poet.

observations.quote: Nil ex omni propte
observations.name: the Poet
observations.note: A Latin margin note, partly illegible, stands at the Poet's saying; it names no person itself.

observations.quote: that man partaker of the Divine Nature, and Lord of all living creatures, should be vexed with Ghosts, and hurryed with Furies
observations.note: Man, though partaker of the Divine Nature and lord of creatures, is vexed and harried; drawn as a consequence from the two sayings, continuing the theme of an enemy set beside power.

observations.quote: in the same place or thing where of his MERCY he appoynted plenty of Physick, even there also by the power of his incomprehensible Justice he substituted Poyson to guard it
observations.name: Roger Bacon
observations.note: Given to Roger Bacon the English Phylosopher: where God's Mercy set Physick, his Justice set Poyson to guard it.

observations.quote: he substituted Poyson to guard it
observations.note: The Physick is guarded by the poison set in the same thing; it is not freely open.

observations.quote: Thistles and prickles of Roses the inseperable companions and avengers of transgressions
observations.note: Thistles and rose prickles are set beside the guarding Poyson as companions and avengers of transgressions; a figure for the poison joined to the good.

observations.quote: Good cannot be known but by evill, and the Enemy being discovered the danger may be avoyded
observations.note: Good is known only through evil, and a discovered enemy can be avoided. The text does not show whether this is still Bacon's or Croll's own.

observations.quote: The severe Justice of God is the disease & venome in all things: on the contrary, the Mercy of God is the Physick in Nature and in all things.
observations.note: The margin note says what the Justice and the Mercy of God are in things: Justice the disease and venom, Mercy the Physick.

observations.name: Wisd.; Eccl.
observations.note: Croll's margin note names places in Wisd. and Eccl. beside the passage given to Roger Bacon.

observations.quote: Holy Hermes the most Ancient Divine (together with Ecclesiasticus) writeth in his Key that all sublunary things ought to consist of contraposition and contrariety
observations.name: Hermes
observations.note: Given to Hermes in a writing called his Key, with Ecclesiasticus named as agreeing: sublunary things consist of contraries.

observations.quote: writeth in his Key
observations.note: A writing of Hermes is named by its title, the Key.

observations.quote: and this after another manner may be of things Impossible in respect of the generation and corruption of things
observations.note: An obscure clause: the contrariety may hold after another manner of things Impossible. It may continue the report of Hermes; the lines given neither explain it nor show whose words they are.

observations.quote: All things that are awlesse are also lawlesse
observations.note: A saying joining being without awe and being without law; it rests on the English pair awlesse and lawlesse. A margin note in foreign script, not transcribed, stands just before it.

observations.quote: nor can Man any other way attaine to the highest pitch unlesse he resolve constantly to maintaine the good fight that is finished in faelicity
observations.note: Man reaches the highest pitch only by constantly maintaining the good fight, which ends in felicity.

observations.quote: God by his Wisdome hath ordained that Sympathy and Antipathy should be alike good
observations.note: Sympathy and Antipathy are ordained by God's Wisdom as alike good, to stir men to search out his secrets.

observations.quote: he would stir up mortall men to contemplate and search out his secrets
observations.note: God has secrets in Nature that men are to search out; the spectacle of Nature is meant to stir them to it.

observations.quote: that if one man hate another, he that is hated might cover and cure the defect of the malicious
observations.note: An application to men: the hated one may cover and cure the defect of the one who hates.

observations.quote: Heraclitus called Nature the daughter of War
observations.name: Heraclitus
observations.note: A name for Nature given to Heraclitus: the daughter of War.

observations.quote: Homer called it Contention
observations.name: Homer
observations.note: A name for Nature given to Homer: Contention.

observations.quote: The cause of Simpathy and Antipathy.
observations.what: The cause of Simpathy and Antipathy
observations.note: The margin note heads the paragraph as giving the cause of Simpathy and Antipathy.

observations.name: Eccl.
observations.note: Croll's margin note names places in Eccl. beside the passage on Sympathy and Antipathy; no verb of saying gives the words to it.

observations.quote: Man is his own enemy; the Cause of dissolution and death in this our Kingdome divided in it selfe, the intestine duell
observations.note: The cause of dissolution and death lies within man himself: a kingdom divided, an intestine duel.

observations.quote: in the little world, the body
observations.note: The text puts the body beside the little world as its meaning here.

observations.quote: in it lyeth hid the preserver and destroyer of health
observations.note: Both what preserves and what destroys health lie hidden in the body, the little world.

observations.quote: the Saints have called the mortall body Hell and Purgatory, wherein continuall war is to be made
observations.name: the Saints
observations.note: Names for the mortal body given to the Saints: Hell and Purgatory.

observations.quote: seeing the Anotomy of Death findeth entertainment in the whole State of our Life
observations.note: The reason given for the Physitians' office: the Anotomy of Death is present through the whole of life. The lines given do not say what the phrase means.

observations.name: Eccl.
observations.note: Croll's margin note names Eccl. 38.15 at the end of the sentence on the body as a place of continual war.

observations.quote: Nature hath commanded the Physitians to be ministers, and to seperate, not masters to compose
observations.note: The Physitian's office is to serve Nature and separate, not to compose as a master.

observations.quote: our Remedies require preparations, separations and exaltations before they can impart their hidden and restrained vertues
observations.note: Three kinds of work are named for remedies: preparations, separations, exaltations; only then do their virtues act.

observations.quote: their hidden and restrained vertues
observations.note: The virtues of remedies are called hidden and restrained until the work frees them.

observations.quote: As all things are proved by Fire, so also the Tryall of the knowledge of Physick is to be made by Fire: Physick and Chymistry cannot be separated
observations.note: Knowledge of Physick is to be tried by Fire, and Physick and Chymistry belong together.

observations.quote: not that which Mountebanks use to paint Faces with to make them White and Red
observations.note: The text sets its Chymistry apart from another thing of the same name, the face-painting of Mountebanks.

observations.quote: doth make manifest, not onely the true Simples, Wonders, Secrets, Mysteries, Vertues, Forces respecting health
observations.note: Chymistry makes manifest what is secret and mysterious in things concerning health.

observations.quote: the Archaeon Ventricle or Naturall In-bred Chymist
observations.note: The Archaeon Ventricle is glossed as the natural in-bred Chymist, which Chymistry imitates.

observations.quote: it teacheth to segregate every mystery into into its own reservacle, and to free the medicines from those scurvy raggs wherein they were wrapt up
observations.note: Two steps: each mystery is set apart into its own reservacle, and the medicines are freed from what wraps them.

observations.quote: to free the medicines from those scurvy raggs wherein they were wrapt up by a due separation from the impurities and corruptible and filthy mixture of superficiall and externall Elements
observations.note: The means of freeing is a due separation from the impure outward mixture of Elements; the result is a pure matter to be given to the body.

observations.quote: that pure and Christiline matter may be administred to our bodies
observations.note: The result of the separation is named a pure, Christiline matter given to the body.

observations.quote: But to deliver this from prison and captivity
observations.note: The pure matter is spoken of as a prisoner to be delivered; with the rags and wrapping this is figure, not plain speech. Freeing it is called a hard task.

observations.quote: Hoc opus, hic labor est
observations.name: UNCLEAR
observations.note: A Latin saying is set in and Englished as a hard task; the text names no source.

observations.quote: without this Chymicall Phylosophy all Physick is but livelesse; Without Alchymicall skill there can be no Speculative or Practick Physick
observations.note: Physick without Chymicall Phylosophy is lifeless; both speculative and practick Physick need Alchymicall skill.

observations.quote: He that rejecteth that knowledge being disheartned by the difficulty thereof shall never find where the disease lyeth
observations.note: Whoever gives up this knowledge for its difficulty will not find where the disease lies.

observations.quote: our common sort of Physitians are not to be followed, who patronize their sloth under other mens paines and study, and use to leave the preparation of their medicines most commonly to some carelesse and covetous Apothecary
observations.note: The common Physitians are not to be followed: charged with sloth, they leave the preparation of medicines to a careless Apothecary, to their patients' harm.

observations.quote: I speake not against the conscientious Apothecaries who by their trusty diligence serve the Common Wealth as the Alchymy of Vulcan
observations.note: Conscientious Apothecaries are excepted and their service likened to the Alchymy of Vulcan; the lines do not explain that name.

observations.quote: By this artificall resolution of bodyes the propertyes which before layd in the compositions of them are now brought to light
observations.note: The work is named a resolution of bodies; it brings to light the properties that lay in their composition.

observations.quote: as by a certaine kinde of artificiall Tynosure, or figures of stars
observations.note: A comparison marked as such: the resolution is like an artificiall Tynosure or figures of stars, by which the Chymists made curtaines to Nature's borders. The sense of the figure is not stated.

observations.quote: this true Analysis and vitall Anatomy of bodies
observations.what: this true Analysis and vitall Anatomy of bodies
observations.note: The same work is named a true Analysis and a vitall Anatomy of bodies, in which a Physitian should be exercised.

observations.quote: this true Analysis and vitall Anatomy of bodies (as hath been said)
observations.note: The text points back to an earlier place where this analysis was spoken of; the place is not named.

observations.quote: there is no constant quality of any body which is not to be found either in the Salt, or Mercury, or Sulphur of the same body
observations.note: Every constant quality of a body is found in its Salt, Mercury or Sulphur.

observations.quote: all compound bodies of the inferiour Globe are to be distributed into three orders or companies; into Animalls, Vegetables, and Mineralls
observations.note: A first step of the work: compound bodies are sorted into three orders before examination.

observations.quote: the individualls of all these, and the parts of the individualls are diligently to be examined
observations.note: The next step: examine the individuals of each order and their parts.

observations.quote: the three First things (viz. Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury)
observations.note: The text says which the three First things are: Salt, Sulphur and Mercury.

observations.quote: For in the shop of Nature there is Animall, Vegetable, Minerall Salt; Animall, vegetable, minerall Sulphur; vegetable, animall, minerall Mercury
observations.note: Each of the three First things is found in each of the three orders, nine in all.

observations.quote: Vegetables comprehend plants, trees, Zoophyts. Animalls are the beasts in their order, creeping swimming, flying, four footed creatures.
observations.note: The margin note says what the orders of Vegetables and Animalls hold, Zoophyts among the Vegetables.

observations.quote: The first face of Things was pure, sound, perfect without corruption and death
observations.note: At first things were pure and without corruption or death.

observations.quote: created all things good by his Will, that all things might glorifie him and live holily and incorruptably according to the prescribed order
observations.note: God made all things good, to glorify him and live incorruptibly.

observations.quote: Man at first was created healthy, (sicknesse entred by the Woman, not by the Man)
observations.note: Man was created healthy; sickness is said to have entered by the Woman.

observations.quote: there appeared two contraries, the externall corruptable, and the internall compleat, which could not long continue in one without unavoydable corruption
observations.note: Death entered because two contraries, an outward corruptible and an inward complete, could not last together in one.

observations.quote: the transgression and fall from unity to alterity
observations.note: The Fall is named a fall from unity to alterity.

observations.quote: by the curse of God new Tinctures came in (even infinite evills)
observations.note: After the fall new Tinctures came in by God's curse; the bracket puts them beside infinite evils.

observations.quote: the beauty of the whole Creature was transplanted
observations.note: The change in the Creature after the fall is called a transplanting; the margin note N169 says what that is.

observations.quote: The transplantation of the Creature is by the calamity and coming in of sicknesse upon it
observations.note: The margin note says what the transplantation of the Creature is: the coming in of sickness upon it.

observations.quote: since the Fall me carry in their own bosome their enemy both of creation and propagation, which causeth sicknesse and death by in-bred contrariety and corruption
observations.note: Since the Fall men carry their enemy within, causing sickness and death by in-bred contrariety; the note echoes Man is his own enemy in CH3.6.

observations.quote: Impurity was joyned to the pure roots, which was the predestination of diseases
observations.note: Impurity joined to the pure roots is called the predestination of diseases.

observations.quote: the roots of sicknesses in certaine individuall or species doe not consist apart by themselves, but are implanted and mixt in the pure and first seeds of things
observations.note: The roots of sicknesses do not stand apart; they are mixed in the pure first seeds of things.

observations.quote: the foure wombs or Elements
observations.note: The four wombs are put beside the Elements as the same; in them spring up the seeds whose fruits are the nourishments.

observations.quote: Nature therefore, as it is now, gives us nothing that is pure in the world, but hath mixed all things with many impurities
observations.note: Nature as it now is gives nothing pure; all is mixed with impurities.

observations.quote: it might often put us in mind that we should begin to learn the knowledge of Chymistry from our cradles
observations.note: The mixture of impurity is a spur of necessity to learn Chymistry from the cradle.

observations.quote: so long as we are shut out of Paradice into the subburbs of this world
observations.note: This world is called the suburbs into which we are shut out of Paradice.

observations.quote: we ought to till and manure the EARTH, to wit, the whole frame of the world
observations.note: The text says what EARTH means here: the whole frame of the world, so the tilling is not meant of soil alone.

observations.quote: both the Visible and Invisible (Limus) Earth
observations.note: The tilling is done by admiration, searching and knowledge; the Earth is twofold, Visible and Invisible, with the Latin word Limus set in brackets beside it.

observations.quote: as Natures Labourers, not lazily, but in the sweat of our browes
observations.note: We are to labour for bread and necessaries as Natures Labourers.

observations.quote: in this LAND of LABOUR to attain the fruits of Terrene and Caelestiall Wisdome
observations.note: The world is named, in capitals, the LAND of LABOUR; the aim of the labour is the fruits of Terrene and Caelestiall Wisdome.

observations.quote: by doing nothing we should learn to doe naughtily
observations.note: Idleness is feared as the teacher of wrongdoing.

observations.quote: this is the true end of Mans Creation, that in the fear of God and love of his neighbor he should manage the Earth, recovering what he hath lost
observations.note: The text announces the true end of man's creation: to manage the Earth and recover what he lost; the Earth here follows the sense given in CH3.12.

observations.quote: the Light of Nature not after his own, but according to the will of his Creator
observations.note: Man is to walk in the Light of Nature according to the Creator's will, not his own.

observations.quote: he should continue the Instrument, Habitation and Tabernacle of God
observations.note: Man is to remain God's instrument, habitation and tabernacle.

observations.quote: he should through Nature search out the wonderfull works of God by consideration of Temporall and Caelestiall observations, thereby to make known the invisible works of God
observations.note: Man is to search out God's works through Nature and so make the invisible works known.

observations.quote: wonders and mysteries which he hath revealed
observations.note: God's works are called mysteries, and they are said to be revealed by him.

observations.quote: He that hath learned to know God & himselfe hath ordered the Earth with good husbandry
observations.note: The margin note makes knowing God and oneself the good husbandry of the Earth, a second sense of the tilling in the paragraphs.

observations.quote: idlenesse the pillow & cushion of the Devill is removed by labour and diligence
observations.note: The margin note sets labour and diligence against idleness, as in CH3.12.

observations.quote: But to passe from Food let us come to Physick
observations.note: The text marks a turn of subject from Food to Physick.

observations.quote: unlesse he had rather eate the husk and shells with the kernell, as the former and more rugged generations have done
observations.note: Refusing the art is likened to eating husk and shells with the kernel, as earlier generations did.

observations.quote: this Separatory art which teacheth rightly to discerne and seperate the Good from the Bad, the Profitable from the Unprofitable
observations.note: The art is named the Separatory art by its work of separating good from bad; a long row of pairs follows.

observations.quote: the Stupefactive from Fire, the minerall Spirit from the Anthos or blossome, the Homogeneans from the Heterogeneans, Poyson from healing Medicines and Balsoms, Light from Darknesse, Life from Death, Day from Night, Visible from Invisible
observations.note: A row of separations the art makes; the order of good and bad within the pairs is not kept the same.

observations.quote: the minerall Spirit from the Anthos or blossome
observations.note: Anthos is glossed as blossome; it stands in the row of things separated, against the minerall Spirit.

observations.quote: that which is pure Celestiall, the kernall and Marrow, from that which is Terrestrial Impure, the Rinds, and Membranes, the Covers, Shells, Husks and dreggs, the Coate aed Cottage of Physick which are enemyes to mans body
observations.note: The pure Celestiall part, the kernel, is covered by the Terrestrial Impure rinds, shells and husks, called the coat and cottage of Physick and enemies to man's body; the same covering named in the chapter heading.

observations.quote: the Soul the Inhabitant thereof, the Super-elementall mystery the Quint-Essence, which is the true Internall, sutable, freindly and correspondent Balsom of our bodyes
observations.note: What dwells within is named in a row of equal names: the Soul, the Super-elementall mystery, the Quint-Essence, the true inner Balsom of our bodies.

observations.quote: that quickning essence may be got, whose faculty mounts more high and quick being loosed from its chaines
observations.note: The aim of the separating is the quickning essence, spoken of as chained and loosed, like the prisoner of CH3.7.

observations.quote: All Venemous things have a Balsom agreeable to Mans Nature, and there is no poysonous Creature but hath in it an Antidote against its own poyson
observations.note: Every venomous thing holds a Balsom fit for man and an antidote to its own poison.

observations.quote: Spiders are good for hens and Sparrowes, Toads for Serpents, Serpents for Staggs and Storks
observations.note: Examples that what is poison to man is food to another creature.

observations.quote: these Formes of Physick work better when they are extracted, then whilst they are drowned in Matter, which alwayes hindereth and restraineth the power and operation of the Secret
observations.note: The Formes of Physick work better extracted than left in Matter; what is extracted is also called the Secret.

observations.quote: Putrefications onely are the true Correctives of all Physick.
observations.note: The margin note names Putrefications alone as the true Correctives of Physick.

observations.quote: Putrefications onely are the true Correctives of all Physick.
observations.note: The note says Putrefications only correct Physick; CH3.20 says the poison of metals is corrected and amended by the help of this Art and of Fire. The same note goes on to give the separating to Fire, so the two may describe different steps.

observations.quote: As Death separateth eternall and perishing things, so doth Fire the good from the bad, the Quint-Essence from the body.
observations.note: The margin note likens Fire to Death: it separates good from bad, the Quint-Essence from the body.

observations.quote: Even the Soule or Form of every kind of thing
observations.note: The text joins Soule and Form as one.

observations.quote: the Soule or Form of every kind of thing hath not onely more, but more excellent vertues and operations by far than either the very body, or the matter of the same thing
observations.note: The Form has more and better virtues than the body or matter of the thing.

observations.quote: as every thing hath its being from the Form, by how much the more it hath of the Form, by so much the more is there of the Entity
observations.note: The reason given: being comes from the Form, so more Form is more Entity.

observations.quote: this the very Enemyes of Chymistry are forced to confess, being compel'd by their own conscience, and convinced thereof by ocular demonstration
observations.name: the very Enemyes of Chymistry
observations.note: Croll says a group, the Enemyes of Chymistry, grant the point when shown it by ocular demonstration; no words of theirs are given.

observations.quote: Hence many advantages follow.
observations.note: Announces a list of advantages; three numbered ones follow in CH3.17 to CH3.19.

observations.quote: Reasons why the Spagyrick Physick duely prepared is to be preferd before other Hetroclite mixtures in the shops.
observations.note: The margin note heads the list as reasons for the Spagyrick Physick over the Hetroclite mixtures of the shops.

observations.quote: First, Because many sick people will take it more easily and willingly
observations.note: First advantage: the sick take it more easily and willingly.

observations.quote: the Physitian himselfe that prescribed it, and the Apothecary that mingled, would abhor and altogether refuse to drink in the like case
observations.note: The common muddy potions, which spoil the complexion, are such that their makers would refuse them.

observations.quote: Secondly, Though these medicines be often used, yet they hurt not the stomack
observations.note: Second advantage: frequent use does not hurt the stomach.

observations.quote: being separate in the stomack, they are by a naturall force carryed without hinderance to their known lodgings
observations.note: The reason given: being separate, they are carried by a natural force to their places, and no harsh earthy parts stay to ulcerate.

observations.quote: Thirdly, Because all the hurtfull quality is altogether cast out of, or at least easily kept under in these Essences
observations.note: Third advantage: the hurtful quality is cast out of the Essences, or kept under by the permixture of other properties.

observations.quote: this Spagyrick art is so necessary that he can be no safe Physitian who hath it not
observations.note: No one is a safe Physitian without the Spagyrick art.

observations.quote: in one simple thinge there are different substances, somtimes of contrary qualityes, whereof one may be hurtfull, the rest healthfull, as we see in Opium and honey
observations.note: One simple may hold substances of contrary qualities, known only by separation; Opium and honey are the examples.

observations.quote: the Galenists may make good their Axioms, who affirm that all bitter things are hot
observations.name: the Galenists
observations.note: An axiom given to the Galenists; the text says only this Art lets them make it good, against the cases of Opium, Roses and Succory.

observations.quote: The knot of this Answer must be cut with an Anatomicall knife fire
observations.note: Fire is called an Anatomicall knife: the cutting is not meant of a blade; anatomy here is separation by fire, as in CH3.8.

observations.quote: thus we come to understand the temperature of simples, by making a seperation of the substances
observations.note: The step: separate the substances of a simple, and so learn its temperature.

observations.quote: in Opium there is a sweet Narcotick Sulphur, and a bitter hot Salt penetrating by a subtile resolution and causing sweat without any stupefactive vertue
observations.note: What the separation of Opium is said to yield: a sweet Narcotick Sulphur and a bitter hot Salt.

observations.quote: yet may it be so corrected and amended by the help of this Art and of Fire, that it may be taken into the whole body without danger
observations.note: The poison of metals can be corrected by this Art and Fire so that it is taken without danger.

observations.quote: as skilfull Physitians well know, who can tell how to pick and cull the best things out of the worst
observations.note: Croll calls on what skilful Physitians know as witness: they draw the best out of the worst.

observations.quote: being of an unruly malignity, yet it is tamed artificially with Salt-Peter, by the assistance of Fire
observations.note: The example given: a malignant thing, its name partly illegible in the transcription, is tamed with Salt-Peter and Fire.

observations.quote: Poyson reduced to its Arcanum is not poyson, but a soveraign nedicine
observations.note: The margin note says what poison becomes when reduced to its Arcanum: a sovereign medicine.

observations.quote: stinking smells by degestion are turned into sweet savours
observations.note: The margin note names degestion as what turns stinking smells sweet; it also speaks of something earthy healed of a leprosy, in words partly illegible.

observations.quote: Mineralls whose spirits exceed ours in subtilty, and precious stones, ought to be accounted medicinable, which rightly prepared doe much excell all Vegetables in effecting cures
observations.note: Minerals and precious stones, rightly prepared, excel all Vegetables in curing; numbered reasons follow.

observations.quote: First, Because so great vertue and strong operations cannot be stampt upon such soft matter, as is that of Plants and living things
observations.note: First reason: the soft matter of plants and living things cannot hold so strong an impression.

observations.quote: Nor can it be that Vegetables which are obnoxious to corruption should so free Mans body from corruption, as the Spirits of perfect mettalls doe
observations.note: The Spirits of perfect mettalls free the body from corruption because they are not subject to it, as Vegetables are.

observations.quote: there being scarce any Oyntment prepared that is not made of an imperfect mettall or minerall
observations.note: Second reason: surgical ointments, nearly all made of an imperfect metal or mineral, show such virtue.

observations.quote: perfect things doubtlesse have received of the Omnipotent far greater force and vertues
observations.note: Drawn from the imperfect to the perfect: perfect things have far greater force.

observations.quote: could by no means so contemper the mixture of those bodies that they should attaine to such admirable power and admit of the solid and stable Nature of a Balsom
observations.note: Third reason: Nature makes living things and plants for many uses, so their mixture cannot reach the solid, stable nature of a Balsom.

observations.quote: Nature therefore by length of time can adorn precious stones and other metallary bodies with a greater faculty of working
observations.note: Fourth reason: the long time of generation gives stones and metallary bodies a greater faculty.

observations.quote: stones require a long time of generation, but perfect bodies are generated in a shorter space
observations.note: Here greater faculty is tied to a long time of generation and perfect bodies are the quicker kind; in CH3.22 and CH3.23 perfect names the metals and things of far greater force. The lines given do not say which bodies are meant here or reconcile the two.

observations.quote: in the Bohemian Garnat is such that it can hardly be spoyled or corrupted by any force of Fire, and that onely because of the fixation of spirits that may be seen in it
observations.note: The Bohemian Garnat resists Fire, and the cause given is the fixation of spirits in it.

observations.quote: may well be preferd before the Orientall Rubie in Physick, which can scarce indure the Fire as many hours as the other can months
observations.note: The Garnat is ranked near Gold and above the Orientall Rubie for Physick, by how long each endures Fire.

observations.quote: This also by the way is to be observed
observations.note: What follows on the stones is marked as an aside.

observations.quote: precious stones have the Colour, Forme and Tincture more or lesse from Mettalls by formation of the Stars, for they are transplanted Mertalls
observations.note: The text says what precious stones are: transplanted metals, taking colour, form and Tincture from metals by the stars.

observations.quote: for they are transplanted Mertalls
observations.note: Transplanted is used here of metals becoming stones, while CH3.11 and N169 use it of the Creature under sickness.

observations.quote: Gemmes are Elementary Stars.
observations.note: The margin note says what Gemmes are: Elementary Stars.

observations.quote: Rubies and Garnats have the Tincture of Gold, Saphirs and Turcoides of Silver, Emeralds and Chrysolites of Copper, the Jacint and Topaz of Iron
observations.note: A list pairing stones with the metal whose Tincture they have.

observations.quote: the Diamond of Tinne-Saturn addeth a gluish matter to the weight or heavinesse
observations.note: The list goes on with the Diamond and Tinne, and with Saturn adding weight; the pointing leaves it unclear where one statement ends and the next begins.

observations.quote: factitious and fictitious gemms that are made of the powder of red lead and white flints proportionably mixed, receiving a mettallick Forme from Fire
observations.note: False gems are made from powder of red lead and white flints mixed in proportion and worked by Fire; offered as proof of the metal in stones.

observations.quote: the skilfull Stone-gravers can easily discerne the cheat and fraud by their softnesse and lightnesse
observations.note: The made gems equal the natural in splendour but are known by softness and lightness.

dropped.reason: Rests on a word left partly unreadable; the text as given does not show what is healed, so a covered meaning cannot be checked. The note's leprosy is mentioned with A112.
Not borne out: CH3.19 does not say the permixture is a composing done by the Physitian, so no conflict with CH3.6 shows in the text.

voices.quote: As soon as the Omnipotent gave Power to Man
voices.basis: The sentence closes with saith Firmianus.

voices.quote: nothing is in every respect happy
voices.basis: Introduced by as the Poet said.
A Latin margin note standing at the Poet's saying; it names no one itself.

voices.quote: that God who made Darknesse and Light
voices.basis: Roger Bacon the English Phylosopher saith; runs to avengers of transgressions.

voices.quote: Good cannot be known but by evill
voices.basis: Follows Bacon's report with no new verb of saying; the text does not show whether it is still Bacon's or Croll's.

voices.quote: that all sublunary things ought to consist of contraposition and contrariety
voices.basis: Holy Hermes ... (together with Ecclesiasticus) writeth in his Key.

voices.quote: and this after another manner may be of things Impossible
voices.basis: Joined to the Hermes report by a semicolon with no new verb of saying; whether Hermes or Croll speaks is not shown.
the Saints have called the mortall body.
A Latin saying set into the sentence; no speaker or writing is named.
